counterexample: Take k = 3 and n = lcm(1,2,3) = 6, so the hypothesis n >= lcm(1,...,k) holds with equality. Line 0009 asserts: if gpf(n+i) <= p_{pi(k)} then some prime power p_i^{v_i} > k divides n+i. For i = 0 this fails: n+0 = 6, gpf(6) = 3 <= p_{pi(3)} = 3, but the maximal prime powers dividing 6 are 2 and 3, neither of which exceeds k = 3. The 'otherwise' argument breaks because it only yields n+i <= lcm(1,...,k) = 6, which is NOT a contradiction when n = lcm(1,...,k) and i = 0 (lcm(1,...,k) is itself a number all of whose maximal prime powers are <= k). Consequently the injection i -> p_i of line 0012 does not exist: the bad indices are i = 0 (6 = 2*3), i = 2 (8 = 2^3), i = 3 (9 = 3^2), i.e. 3 indices, while only pi(3) = 2 primes <= 3 are available. The theorem's conclusion itself is false here: [n, n+k] = {6,7,8,9} contains only ONE integer with a prime factor > 3 (namely 7), whereas the theorem of line 0005 claims at least k+1-pi(k) = 3+1-2 = 2. The Grimm corollary (line 0014) fails on the same instance: 7 -> 7, 8 -> 2, 9 -> 3 exhausts the usable primes and leaves 6 with no distinct prime. (Same failure at k = 2, n = lcm(1,2) = 2: {2,3,4} has only one integer, 3, with a prime factor > 2, but the claim demands 2+1-pi(2) = 2.)
reasoning_summary: The rewritten theorem in line 0005 is stated with the non-strict hypothesis n >= lcm(1,...,k). The key step 0009 derives, from gpf(n+i) <= p_{pi(k)}, the existence of a prime power p_i^{v_i} > k dividing n+i, by arguing that otherwise n+i <= prod_{p<=k} p^{r_p} = lcm(1,...,k). That contradiction requires n+i > lcm(1,...,k), which fails exactly at the boundary n = lcm(1,...,k), i = 0 -- and lcm(1,...,k) is precisely a number every maximal prime power of which is <= k, so the conclusion of 0009 is genuinely false there, not merely unproved. The failure is not a mere technicality: it kills the theorem's conclusion. For k = 3, n = 6 the interval {6,7,8,9} has only one integer (7) with a prime factor exceeding 3, while the theorem asserts at least 2. The counting/injection argument of lines 0010-0012 correspondingly over-assigns: three indices (0, 2, 3) have gpf <= 3 but only two primes <= 3 exist. The corollary on Grimm's conjecture (line 0014) inherits the same failure on the same instance. Fixing the statement to n > lcm(1,...,k) (or the Langevin-style condition that no n+i divides lcm(1,...,k), which the answer itself mentions in line 0026) would repair it, but the proof as written and as stated is invalid.
